title: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
chapter: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
goal: Worked example: why one order always wins by the same amount.

scenes.visual: Set up two unsolved operation machines using the same whole-number input.
scenes.narration: Start with any whole number, including zero. Rule A adds three and then multiplies by four. Rule B multiplies by four and then adds three. Which output is larger, and by how much? Sketch one example before looking for a proof.

scenes.visual: Copy the whole x plus three bar four times, then display four x tiles and four threes.
scenes.narration: Call the start x. Rule A forms x plus three and makes four copies of the whole amount. Look at one copy. It contains an x tile and a three tile. Four copies give four x tiles and four threes, so the result is four x plus twelve.

scenes.visual: Copy x alone four times. Bring in one gold three from the add step.
scenes.narration: In Rule B, the multiplication acts on the starting value. Make four copies of x. Now add the three. This time the three comes in once, after the copying step. The result is four x plus three.

scenes.visual: Align the two rows, dim each matched x and matching three, then collect the unmatched gold pieces.
scenes.narration: Line up the outputs. Each side contains four copies of the same x and one added three. Pair those tiles. There are three extra threes in Rule A. Their total is nine. Whatever whole number we pick at the start, Rule A is larger by nine.

scenes.visual: Use an input-output table to check zero and ten with the proved difference.
scenes.narration: Check the smallest allowed input. Starting from zero gives twelve and three. Starting from ten gives fifty-two and forty-three. Each difference is nine. In both rows, the starting amount changes the two outputs by the same amount.

scenes.visual: Draw the repeatable copy rule, then present the add two and multiply by six challenge.
scenes.narration: The multiplication makes extra copies of the added amount when the addition comes first. Use that observation with two new rules. One adds two before multiplying by six. The other multiplies by six before adding two. Draw the matching pieces and find the gap.

notebook_exercise: Find the gap between "add 2 then multiply by 6" and "multiply by 6 then add 2".
